I distract myself with something else

Being superalert or watchful or on guard

My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

issues.explanation: Occupation 'Retired' is implausible for age 28 (retired is implausible if age < 50).

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within Memory, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' sits awkwardly with 'my memories are very clear and detailed' and 'mostly pictures or images' for a PTSD profile tied to a life-threatening accident; this pattern suggests unusually easy verbal processing despite vivid intrusive-style memory, which weakens coherence of the memory node.

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: The threat item about repeatedly checking whether someone is following him implies an interpersonal pursuit/assault-type danger theme, which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma being a life-threatening accident and with the rest of the profile, which does not otherwise indicate persecution-related threat.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: 'I dwell on what other people have done to me' also implies an interpersonal harm/blame theme that does not fit well with the accident trauma context or the other selected appraisals, memories, and threats.

issues.item: Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
issues.explanation: Restricting food as a coping strategy is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The other items describe accident-related sensory threat (loud sounds, startle), image-based trauma memory, and self-critical appraisals, with maladaptive responses centered on avoidance/removal from reminders and rumination/meaning seeking. Undereating introduces a qualitatively different coping pattern that is not reflected elsewhere in Triggers, Threat, Memory, or Negative Appraisals, making it the least clinically coherent item in this five-component profile.

vignette: Thomas, a 52‑year‑old European film director, remembers the night the world narrowed to a single, dark cabin on a rain‑slick highway. The car he had driven to a remote shoot site skidded off the road, the engine sputtered, and he was thrown into a silent, oppressive darkness that lasted for what felt like an eternity. The image of his own reflected eyes in the cracked glass, the muffled thud of the impact, the scent of wet earth—these pictures replay in his mind with brutal clarity, a vivid memory that never fades. Thomas thinks about why this terrible event happened to him, the way his mind has begun to ask, “Why me?” that question haunts him, fueling an appraisal that he feels inadequate, a bad cop, and that he has become unrecognisable. Those negative appraisals do more than sit in his thoughts; they push him to adopt a handful of maladaptive strategies: he now shuns any circumstance that reminds him of the accident, particularly darkness; he seeks meaning in every possible explanation, often sitting alone for hours trying to piece together why fate had chosen him; and he distracts himself with the meticulous planning of his next shoot, turning his creative mind into a shield. The constant threat that hangs over Thomas is palpable. An unexpected creak of the set’s rigging or the sudden clang of a camera tripod is enough to set his heart racing; he feels a high alert when any sound seems too loud or too sudden. Because of the relentless hypervigilance and the startle response that catches him off guard at ordinary noises, he is on guard all the time, a state that fuels and is fueled by his fear of darkness and loud sounds. This threat compels him to avoid the very situations that might restore him to the world he once knew. The avoidance becomes a strategy, a way to keep the terror at bay. The more he relies on these avoidance habits, the deeper the threat feels, a loop that tightens with each missed opportunity to confront the past. In the days that followed the crash, Thomas would skip night shoots, leave the studio early, and whenever a bright flash of a flashbulb or a sudden hiss of a camera’s shutter startled him, he would instinctively flee the scene, his sense of safety continually on a precipice. Thomas’s memories of that night, the vivid images of the car’s broken side, the smell of burnt plastic, the cold of the cabin’s interior, feed back into his perception of threat. The clarity of these memories means that a sudden noise—a clatter from the crew’s equipment or a siren in the distance—can instantly conjure that night’s terror. The same vivid images also deepen his negative appraisals. He is convinced that the world is now a dangerous place that rewards him with peril rather than purpose, and this conviction hardens his sense of inadequacy. As his maladaptive strategies intensify—his avoidance of dark environments, his relentless search for meaning, his constant mental redirection—his memories become more intrusive, and he finds himself revisiting that cabin in his mind at random, the images sharpening each time. His strategies of avoidance and distraction, in turn, reinforce his negative self‑view; he feels as if he cannot cope, that he has failed both as a director and as a person. The cycle that binds his memory to his threat, his threat to his maladaptive strategies, and his maladaptive strategies back to his memory and negative appraisals has tightened with every sleepless night and every skipped meeting with his partner. The film set is where Thomas’s avoidance becomes most evident. He refuses to work on projects that require night shoots, fearing the black darkness that once trapped him. When the crew’s director of photography begins a sudden test of a new strobe light, Thomas’s heart races; the bright flash triggers the same vivid image of the cabin’s glass, and he stumbles out of the control room, leaving a crucial scene unfinished. His partner, who has watched his anxiety grow, often offers gentle reminders that the darkness on the set is merely artificial and controllable, but Thomas feels that his mind cannot separate reality from the nightmare. The repeated avoidance has begun to strain his relationship; he feels increasingly distant, as if he is retreating into a self‑constructed barrier to keep the pain at bay. Now, after months of sleepless nights, of frantic workdays punctuated by the abrupt startle of a clack, Thomas finally seeks help. What has pushed him to this point is the relentless erosion of his creative confidence and the growing sense that his identity as a film director—his life’s work—is slipping away. He fears that his avoidance will become a permanent wall that isolates him from the very stories he wants to tell. At the same time, he hopes to reclaim the ability to navigate a world that no longer feels like a constant threat, to stand on a set without the heart racing at a simple echo of a camera shutter. In the quiet moments between meetings, Thomas clutches the memory of that dark cabin, aware that he is caught in a loop that has left him feeling inadequate and unrecognisable, but he also yearns for the day when the lights on set will no longer flash like a warning sign but simply illuminate a new scene.
